title: Huntington to Babylon: A Sequence of Land Claims
summary: The 1653 First Purchase was one step in a longer expansion toward the south shore. Later acquisitions, disputes and colonial patents helped turn Native homeland into town-held and privately allotted property.
address_label: Approximate historical landscape — not a visitor entrance
map_geometry_source: Modern regional context, not a historic deed survey. NYS town outline and land mask; historical comparisons and retained-land qualifications in Location section. Reviewed September 26, 2026.
why_this_matters: Land loss was a process involving agreements, contested claims, colonial institutions and restrictions on Native access. Read the actors, obligations and continuing communities together; a broad outline does not mean every Native right ended on one date.
introduction_title: Native homeland, colonial claims and continuing rights
introduction_content: The 1653 First Purchase was one step in a longer expansion toward the south shore. Later acquisitions, disputes and colonial patents helped turn Native homeland into town-held and privately allotted property.
history_title: How control of the land changed
history_content:
From the north shore toward the Great South Bay

The first Huntington purchase in 1653 was one step in a much longer transformation of Native land. It concerned a north-shore landscape associated with Matinecock people, not the whole north-to-south area that colonists later called Huntington. That larger colonial town also encompassed land in today's Babylon. Vanishing Tidelands: Land Use and the Law in Suffolk County, NY 1650–1979

Several acquisitions, not one sale

Raseokan's agreement with Richard Holbrook, Robert Williams and Daniel Whitehead was followed by further acquisitions. Kavenagh's historical reconstruction maps a sequence extending into the early eighteenth century, including southern tracts toward the Great South Bay. Showing all of this as a single 1653 sale would erase both the chronology and the separate transactions through which the colonial claim expanded. Vanishing Tidelands: Land Use and the Law in Suffolk County, NY 1650–1979

Competing claims and Native objections

Purchasers and colonial towns also disagreed among themselves. Huntington's eastern claim overlapped Richard Smith's claim near the Nissequogue River. The later court settlement helped define Smithtown and Huntington, but a decision between colonists should not be mistaken for a new agreement with every Native owner. The adjoining Smithtown records preserve a Native complaint that Smith had taken land and agreements reserving Native rights. Those are part of the same regional story of disputed authority. Records of the Town of Smithtown, Long Island, N.Y.

How paper claims changed control of land

English government added another layer after taking New Netherland in 1664. Colonial patents confirmed claims under the governor's authority. Huntington's town institutions allocated land among proprietors and later trustees administered town-held land. These arrangements made the deed claims consequential: they provided mechanisms for dividing land, settling families, regulating access and passing property onward. The transition was not accomplished by one signature alone. The Early Years

The homeland story continues

The separate 1653 First Purchase area and this wider region tell different parts of the same history. Native names and continuing homeland connections belong beside the colonial records. An expanding paper title is not evidence that Native people ceased to exist, and the transactions did not all have identical terms. Vanishing Tidelands: Land Use and the Law in Suffolk County, NY 1650–1979

Read the 1653 First Purchase, Matinecock Ancestral Land and Secatogue Ancestral Land.
whereintheworld_content:
The polygon joins the present-day Huntington and Babylon regions as an orientation area for the longer acquisition sequence. It is not a single deed boundary or an assertion that all Native rights ended on one date. Kavenagh’s map 2 distinguishes purchases and disputes from 1653 to 1705. The modern outline also includes Lloyd Neck, whose jurisdiction was not transferred to Huntington until 1885; it is included here for orientation, not attributed to Huntington’s 1653 purchase. Open the separate First Purchase area for that smaller, approximately reconstructed tract.
